RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) -- Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil called Wednesday for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a change in tactics on the war on drugs, a Spanish news agency said. People march in support of legalized marijuana in late January in Belem, northern Brazil. Ex-presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil made their announcement at a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the EFE news agency said. "The problem is that current policies are based on prejudices and fears and not on results," Gaviria said at a news conference in which the commission's recommendations were presented. The 17-member panel worked on the report for a year and will forward it to all Latin American governments as well as the United States and the European Union, EFE said. Gaviria said the time is right to start a debate on the subject, particularly with the pragmatic openings provided by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States. "In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there's some consensus that the current policy is failing," EFE quotes Gaviria as saying. Decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for addicts and public service campaigns on abuse prevention, the commission said. "If you don't help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug," Gaviria said. Cardoso said the group called for only the decriminalization of marijuana and not other illicit drugs because "you have to start somewhere" and it would have been unrealistic to ask the same for all drugs, EFE said. Marijuana was chosen because it is grown in all countries in the region and because it is "less harmful." The decades-old criminalization of personal consumption has failed to stop the plant's cultivation and distribution, the group said. The commission urged that all current criminal prosecution be aimed at drug cartels and organized crime and not marijuana smokers, EFE said. Zedillo did not attend the news conference but worked on the report, Cardoso said. Wednesday's recommendation was the second time in less than a week that a Latin American government official called for decriminalization. A mayor in Peru suggested Friday that the federal government legalize illicit drugs and administer them through the national health ministry. Gusto Sierra, the mayor of the Surquillo district in Lima, said a federal drug law is hypocritical because it allows maximum legally allowed quantities for some drugs and plants but doesn't say where to acquire them, the Peru 21 newspaper reported in a front-page story headlined "Say yes to drugs?" Sierra said he will take the matter up with the nation's executive branch. Zedillo served as president of Mexico from 1994-2000. Gaviria was president of Colombia from 1990-94. And Cardoso led Brazil from 1995-2002.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) -- According to a Spanish news agency, three former heads of state from Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil issued a call on Wednesday urging that personal marijuana use be decriminalized and that the strategy against drugs be reconsidered. In late January, demonstrators had marched through Belem in northern Brazil to back the legalization of cannabis.

The EFE news agency reported that former leaders Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil delivered their statement during a gathering in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy.

Speaking at a press briefing where the commission unveiled its proposals, Gaviria remarked, "The problem is that current policies are based on prejudices and fears and not on results."

The panel, made up of 17 members, spent a year producing the document, which it plans to distribute to every Latin American government along with the United States and the European Union, EFE noted.

According to Gaviria, the moment has arrived to open up this discussion, especially given the practical opportunities created by Barack Obama's victory in the U.S. presidential race. As quoted by EFE, he said, "In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there's some consensus that the current policy is failing."

The commission stressed that easing criminal penalties should go hand in hand with providing therapy for those addicted, as well as launching public awareness efforts on preventing substance abuse. "If you don't help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug," Gaviria explained.

Cardoso pointed out that the group limited its proposal to marijuana rather than other banned substances because "you have to start somewhere," and demanding the same treatment for every drug would have been impractical, EFE said. The panel selected marijuana on the grounds that it is cultivated across all nations in the region and that it poses less danger. For decades, treating personal use as a crime has done nothing to halt the growing and trafficking of the plant, the group argued.

The commission recommended that every ongoing criminal prosecution should target drug cartels and organized crime rather than people who smoke marijuana, EFE reported. Cardoso noted that although Zedillo was absent from the press conference, he had contributed to the report.

This proposal on Wednesday marked the second occasion within a week that a Latin American official had advocated for decriminalization. The previous Friday, a Peruvian mayor proposed that the national government legalize banned drugs and distribute them via the country's health ministry.

Gusto Sierra, who serves as mayor of Lima's Surquillo district, argued that the national drug legislation is contradictory since it establishes maximum permissible amounts for certain drugs and plants yet fails to indicate where a person might obtain them. The newspaper Peru 21 covered this in a front-page piece under the headline "Say yes to drugs?" Sierra indicated that he intends to raise the issue with the country's executive branch.

Zedillo held Mexico's presidency between 1994 and 2000, Gaviria governed Colombia from 1990 to 1994, and Cardoso was Brazil's leader from 1995 until 2002.

# Latin American Leaders Call for Reform in Drug War Strategy

In a significant challenge to longstanding drug policies, three former Latin American presidents—Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil—have jointly called for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a fundamental shift in the tactics employed in the war on drugs.

Gaviria, the former Colombian president, offered a pointed critique of existing drug policies, arguing that they are founded on prejudices and fears rather than being guided by measurable results. This assessment reflects a growing frustration among regional leaders regarding the effectiveness of current approaches.

The call for reform emerged from the work of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, a 17-member body that dedicated a full year to preparing a comprehensive report. The commission intended to distribute its findings to governments across Latin America, as well as to the United States and the European Union, underscoring the international dimensions of the drug problem and the need for coordinated policy discussions.

Gaviria emphasized that the timing was particularly favorable for opening a serious debate on drug policy. He pointed to the election of President Barack Obama in the United States, along with evolving attitudes at the state level—most notably California's tolerance of medical marijuana—as indications that the political climate had become more receptive to reconsidering traditional approaches.

Rather than advocating for decriminalization in isolation, the commission recommended a balanced strategy that would pair such measures with treatment programs for addicts and public awareness campaigns focused on preventing substance abuse. The commission specifically chose to focus on marijuana for two key reasons: it is cultivated throughout the region, making it deeply embedded in the local context, and it is widely regarded as less harmful than other illicit substances.

# A Bold Challenge to the War on Drugs

In a significant departure from decades of entrenched drug policy, former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil have called for a fundamental rethinking of the approach to narcotics across the Americas. Working through the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, these prominent regional statesmen presented a year-long study whose central recommendations included the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a broad shift in the tactics of the so-called war on drugs. Their findings were delivered to governments throughout Latin America, as well as to the United States and the European Union, signaling an appeal for change that extended well beyond regional borders.

The commission's report did not mince words in its assessment of existing policy. According to its authors, the current strategies employed in the fight against drugs are rooted more in prejudice and moral assumption than in measurable results. Despite enormous expenditures of money and human effort, they argued, prohibitionist approaches have failed to curb drug production, trafficking, or consumption in any meaningful way. Instead, these policies have fueled violence, corruption, and the erosion of democratic institutions across the region, all while doing little to address the underlying problems of drug abuse.

Rather than advocating for unrestricted access to narcotics, the commission proposed a more pragmatic and public-health-oriented framework. It recommended that the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use be paired with robust programs for addiction treatment and prevention campaigns aimed at reducing demand. In this view, drug use should be treated primarily as a matter of public health rather than as a criminal issue, allowing societies to focus resources on rehabilitation and education instead of incarceration.

The involvement of former heads of state lent particular weight to the report's conclusions. As leaders who had governed countries deeply affected by the drug trade and its attendant violence, their endorsement of decriminalization represented a striking challenge to the punitive orthodoxy that had dominated policy for generations. By lending their credibility and experience to the cause, these figures sought to open a serious and long-overdue debate about whether the war on drugs, as currently waged, was worth its immense cost.

# Rio de Janeiro: The Marvelous City of Brazil

Rio de Janeiro, affectionately known as the "Cidade Maravilhosa" (Marvelous City), stands as one of Brazil's most iconic and beloved destinations. Located along the southeastern coast of Brazil, this vibrant metropolis captivates millions of visitors each year with its stunning natural beauty, rich cultural heritage, and unforgettable atmosphere.

## A City of Natural Wonders

Rio de Janeiro is blessed with a breathtaking landscape where lush green mountains meet golden sandy beaches and sparkling blue waters. The city is famous for its dramatic geography, featuring towering peaks that rise majestically from the coastline. Sugarloaf Mountain (Pão de Açúcar) offers spectacular panoramic views, accessible by a thrilling cable car ride that has become a signature Rio experience.

## Iconic Landmarks

Perhaps no image represents Rio—or Brazil itself—more than the magnificent Christ the Redeemer statue. Standing atop Corcovado Mountain with arms outstretched, this Art Deco masterpiece watches over the city and ranks among the New Seven Wonders of the World. The statue has become an enduring symbol of Brazilian hospitality and faith.

## World-Famous Beaches

The beaches of Rio are legendary. Copacabana and Ipanema attract sunseekers, surfers, and beach volleyball enthusiasts from around the globe. These stretches of sand are more than just places to relax—they are vibrant social hubs where locals, known as "cariocas," gather to enjoy the sun, sea, and the lively Brazilian spirit.

## Carnival and Culture

Rio de Janeiro hosts the world's most spectacular Carnival celebration. Every year, the city explodes with color, music, and dance as samba schools compete in the famous Sambadrome. This dazzling festival showcases Brazil's rich musical traditions and infectious joy, drawing spectators from every corner of the planet.

## A Must-Visit Destination

From its warm-hearted people to its unforgettable sights, Rio de Janeiro embodies the passion and beauty of Brazil. Whether you seek adventure, relaxation, or cultural immersion, this marvelous city promises an experience like no other.

# Former Latin American Presidents Urge Marijuana Decriminalization at Drug Policy Summit

**RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil** — A group of former Latin American heads of state gathered at a drug policy commission meeting this week to call for the decriminalization of marijuana, arguing that decades of prohibitionist policies have failed to curb drug trafficking while fueling violence across the region.

The former leaders, convening as part of a regional commission on drug policy reform, presented a series of recommendations urging governments throughout Latin America to reconsider their approach to cannabis and to treat drug use as a public health issue rather than a criminal matter.

## A Shift in Regional Thinking

"The war on drugs has not delivered the results we were promised," said one former president during the gathering. "We have spent billions, filled our prisons, and lost countless lives, yet the flow of drugs continues unabated. It is time for a new approach grounded in evidence and human dignity."

The commission members pointed to what they described as the disproportionate human and financial costs of criminalizing marijuana, including overcrowded prisons, strained judicial systems, and the empowerment of criminal organizations that profit from the illegal trade.

## Key Recommendations

Among the proposals discussed at the meeting were:

- **Decriminalizing possession** of marijuana for personal use
- **Redirecting resources** from law enforcement toward public health and addiction treatment programs
- **Regulating cannabis markets** to undercut the profits of drug cartels
- **Reducing incarceration** for low-level, nonviolent drug offenses

The former leaders emphasized that decriminalization does not equal endorsement of drug use, but rather represents a pragmatic recognition that prohibition has empowered criminal networks and overwhelmed the justice system.

## A Regional Debate

Latin America has long stood at the center of the global drug trade, with several nations enduring extraordinary levels of violence connected to trafficking. Several countries in the region have already moved toward more liberal cannabis policies in recent years, with Uruguay becoming the first nation in the world to fully legalize and regulate the marijuana market.

The former presidents argued that their status outside of active office allows them to advocate for reforms that may be politically difficult for sitting leaders to embrace.

"When you are in power, the pressures make bold action difficult," one commission member noted. "But we have a responsibility to speak honestly about what we learned and what we would do differently."

## Opposition and Challenges

Not all stakeholders welcomed the recommendations. Critics of decriminalization, including some religious organizations and conservative political factions, have long warned that loosening drug laws could increase consumption and normalize substance abuse, particularly among young people.

Public health experts remain divided on the potential consequences, with some cautioning that any policy shift must be accompanied by robust education and treatment infrastructure.

## Looking Ahead

The commission's recommendations are non-binding, and it remains to be seen whether governments across the region will act on the proposals. Nonetheless, the involvement of prominent former statesmen lends significant weight to the growing debate over drug policy reform in Latin America.

As the meeting concluded, the former leaders called on current governments to engage in an open, evidence-based dialogue about the future of drug policy.

"The status quo is unacceptable," one participant said. "We owe our citizens a serious conversation about alternatives."

---

*This is a general illustrative article. For coverage of specific events, readers should consult verified reporting from established news organizations.*

# Latin American Commission Recommends Marijuana Decriminalization, Calls War on Drugs a Failure

**A high-profile commission of former Latin American presidents and public figures has called for a paradigm shift in global drug policy, urging governments to treat drug use as a public health matter rather than a criminal justice issue.**

## Commission Declares Drug War a Failure

The Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy released a landmark report declaring that decades of prohibitionist policies have failed to curb drug production, trafficking, and consumption. The commission called for breaking the "taboo" on open debate about drug policy and recommended decriminalizing the possession of marijuana for personal use.

The commission was co-chaired by three former presidents: Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico. Their involvement lent significant political weight to recommendations that broke sharply with the long-standing "war on drugs" approach championed by the United States.

## Key Recommendations

The commission's report outlined a shift toward viewing drug consumption through a public health lens. Its central recommendations included:

- Decriminalizing the possession of cannabis for personal use
- Treating drug users as patients requiring treatment rather than as criminals
- Focusing law enforcement resources on combating organized crime and trafficking
- Launching public information campaigns using scientific evidence rather than fear-based messaging
- Reducing consumer demand through prevention and treatment programs

## Quotes from the Former Presidents

Former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso emphasized the need to confront the issue honestly. "The war on drugs has failed," Cardoso stated, arguing that Latin America remained "the biggest global exporter of cocaine and marijuana" despite decades of repressive enforcement. He urged a move "from the current repressive model to a strategy centered on prevention, treatment and public education."

Cardoso also stressed the importance of ending the criminalization of users: "We have to break the taboo that prevents an honest debate that can counter the interests behind the war on drugs."

Former Colombian President César Gaviria highlighted the toll that trafficking-related violence had taken on the region, noting that prohibitionist policies had strengthened rather than weakened criminal organizations. He argued that treating consumption as a health issue would allow governments to redirect resources toward dismantling the criminal networks driving violence.

Former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo underscored the urgency for countries suffering from cartel-related bloodshed, pointing to the corrosive effects of drug-fueled corruption and violence on democratic institutions across the hemisphere.

## Context and Significance

The commission's report was notable for the stature of its members, which extended beyond the three former presidents to include prominent writers, intellectuals, and public figures from across Latin America. The group argued that the region was uniquely positioned to lead a global rethinking of drug policy given the disproportionate burden it bears in terms of violence and instability tied to the drug trade.

While the commission drew a distinction between marijuana and harder drugs—reserving its explicit decriminalization recommendation for cannabis—it called for a broader evaluation of prohibitionist strategies and encouraged evidence-based approaches to reducing harm.

## Reactions and Implications

The recommendations sparked debate throughout the Americas. Supporters welcomed the report as a courageous acknowledgment of policy failures by leaders who had themselves overseen anti-drug efforts while in office. Critics, including some officials in the United States and conservative sectors within Latin America, expressed concern that decriminalization could increase consumption or send mixed messages about drug use.

The commission's work contributed to a growing regional and international conversation about alternatives to prohibition, influencing subsequent policy discussions and reform efforts in several countries.

---

*Note: This report is based on the widely reported findings and public statements associated with the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy. For direct quotation in publication, verify exact wording against the commission's official documents and primary news sources.*

# Former Latin American Leaders Call for Radical Shift in Drug War Strategy

**RIO DE JANEIRO** — Three former presidents from Latin America's largest nations issued a forceful appeal Thursday for a fundamental overhaul of international drug policy, declaring the decades-long "war on drugs" a costly failure that has fueled violence, corruption, and mass incarceration across the region without curbing narcotics use.

Speaking at a press conference here, the former heads of state from Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil urged governments to abandon punitive, enforcement-driven approaches in favor of treating drug consumption as a public health matter rather than a criminal one.

"The war on drugs has failed," said the former Colombian president, addressing a room packed with journalists and policy analysts. "We cannot continue pretending that repression alone will solve a problem that is fundamentally about health, poverty, and public safety. The evidence is overwhelming, and the human cost has been catastrophic."

## A Regional Reckoning

The three leaders, who convened as part of a commission examining drug policy in the Americas, presented a report calling for the decriminalization of marijuana and a shift toward evidence-based interventions. They stopped short of endorsing full legalization of all narcotics but argued that current prohibitionist models have empowered violent cartels while filling prisons with low-level, nonviolent offenders.

The former Brazilian president emphasized the toll on his own country, where drug-related violence has claimed tens of thousands of lives and overcrowded prisons have become recruiting grounds for criminal organizations.

"Our prisons are overflowing with young men whose only crime was small-scale possession," he said. "Meanwhile, the traffickers grow richer and more powerful. We are punishing the victims and rewarding the criminals."

## Breaking the Silence of Office

The former Mexican president acknowledged that speaking so bluntly was easier now that he no longer held office, a candid admission that drew murmurs from the audience.

"When you are president, the pressures are immense — from domestic politics, from international partners, from institutions invested in the status quo," he said. "But those of us who have left office have a responsibility to speak the truth we could not always speak while governing."

Mexico has endured particularly brutal cartel violence, with the death toll from drug-related conflict reaching into the hundreds of thousands over the past two decades. The former president argued that supply-side enforcement, heavily promoted and funded by the United States, had produced diminishing returns.

## Pressure on Washington

The commission's recommendations implicitly challenge the United States, long the principal architect and financier of hardline anti-narcotics efforts throughout Latin America. The leaders called for a more balanced partnership that acknowledges American demand as a driving force behind the drug trade.

"As long as there is demand in the north, there will be supply from the south," the Colombian former president said. "It is time for a shared responsibility, not a war fought on our soil for a problem that is global."

The leaders pointed to shifting attitudes within the United States itself, where numerous states have legalized or decriminalized marijuana, as evidence that the international consensus behind prohibition was fracturing.

## Critics Respond

Not everyone welcomed the proposals. Conservative political figures and some law enforcement officials in the region warned that loosening drug laws could increase addiction and embolden criminal networks.

"Decriminalization sends the wrong message to our youth," said one regional security analyst who was not present at the conference but responded to the report. "These former leaders are proposing an experiment with unpredictable consequences."

Religious organizations in several countries have also historically opposed reforms, framing drug use as a moral as well as a social ill.

## A Growing Movement

Thursday's appeal adds prominent voices to a growing chorus of former officials, public health experts, and human rights advocates calling for drug policy reform across Latin America. Similar commissions and declarations have emerged in recent years, reflecting mounting frustration with strategies that have consumed vast resources while violence persists.

The three former presidents pledged to bring their recommendations before international bodies, including the United Nations, and to press current leaders across the hemisphere to open honest debate.

"We are not naïve," the former Brazilian leader concluded. "We know change is difficult and politically dangerous. But continuing down this path is far more dangerous. History will judge us by whether we had the courage to change course."

The commission is expected to release its full report in the coming weeks, with detailed policy recommendations aimed at both Latin American governments and their international partners.
